front: RPC: what reference paper and OSTEP chapter back this lecture?
back:
• Paper: Implementing Remote Procedure Calls, Birrell & Nelson.
  • OSTEP chapter 48, Distributed Systems.

front: Why RPC: what did the two example applications (get a file; send an image for processing) have in common that motivated RPC?
back: Their client/server setup steps were very similar, even identical at points; the only real differences were the request made and the data transmitted. Almost all basic client/server programs repeat this setup, so simplifying it gave rise to RPC in the 1980s, as networks got faster and distributed applications multiplied. With sockets the developer explicitly creates and initializes sockets, allocates buffers, fills them with protocol information (e.g. a "get file" directive, the buffer size), and copies data in and out.

front: RPC in one sentence: what is it intended to simplify?
back: The development of interactions across address spaces and machines.

front: List the three benefits of RPC.
back:
• High-level interface for data movement and communication, so the developer focuses on what the application does rather than boilerplate setup.
  • Handles many low-level communication/transmission errors, so each program need not re-implement error handling.
  • Hides the complexities of cross-machine interactions: the machines may be of different types, the network between them may fail, and the machines themselves may fail.

front: RPC requirements: what IPC interaction model is RPC designed for?
back: Client/server interactions: the server performs some complex task, and the clients need not have the server's capabilities or access to the same data; they only need to be able to issue requests to the server for whatever they need.

front: RPC call semantics: what happens to the calling process when it makes a remote procedure call, and why this semantics?
back: RPCs have synchronous call semantics: the caller blocks until the procedure completes and returns, exactly like a local procedure call. Most languages at the time were procedural, which set this expectation.

front: RPC and type checking: what does it give you besides catching wrong-type arguments?
back: Type checking lets the RPC runtime optimize its implementation: packets between machines are just a stream of bytes, so carrying type information helps the runtime interpret those bytes. Passing a wrong-type argument yields an error.

front: RPC data representation: why is cross-machine conversion needed, and how is it handled?
back: Client and server may differ in endianness, floating point representation, negative-number representation, and so on. The RPC system hides these differences; one approach is for the runtime and both endpoints to agree on a single representation (e.g. everything represented in network format), so no per-call negotiation is needed.

front: RPC requirements: why is RPC meant to be more than a transport-level protocol?
back: It should support different underlying protocols (UDP, TCP, others) and also incorporate higher-level mechanisms like access control, authentication, and fault tolerance (e.g. if a server does not respond, the client can retry the same request, to the same server or to a replica).

front: RPC timeouts: lecture says RPC call semantics should mirror local calls; what does Birrell & Nelson do about limiting a call's duration?
back: The paper follows "semantics as close as possible to local procedure calls" so strictly that it provides no time-out limiting a call's duration in the absence of machine or communication failures, because local calls have none (Sec. 1.4).

front: Structure of RPC: in the calculator example, who holds the implementation of the operation and who sends the data?
back: The client sends the operation it wants plus the data to the server; the server (the calculator) holds the implementation and performs the operation on the client's behalf. RPC abstracts away the low-level communication/transport details.

front: Client stub: when the client calls add(i,j) without holding add's implementation, where does execution jump?
back: To a stub implementation in the client's address space, not to the real add. To the rest of the process the stub looks like the real add.

front: Client stub: what is its responsibility for an RPC call?
back: Create a buffer and populate it with the function name (add) and the arguments (i, j); then the RPC runtime sends the buffer to the server (e.g. over TCP/IP sockets or another transport protocol).

front: Stub code: who writes it?
back: Nobody by hand; the stub code is automatically generated by tools that are part of the RPC package. The programmer does not write it.

front: Server stub: what does it do when packets arrive, through returning the result?
back:
• Parses the received bytes and determines this is an RPC request for add with i and j.
  • Calls the local add in the server process with those arguments.
  • The server creates a result buffer and sends it back; the client stub receives it, stores it in the client address space, and the client function returns.

front: Five pieces of program: lecture describes a client stub and server stub; what five pieces does Birrell & Nelson name, and how are they split across machines?
back: The user, user-stub, RPCRuntime, server-stub, and server. User, user-stub, and one RPCRuntime run on the caller machine; server, server-stub, and another RPCRuntime run on the callee machine (Sec. 1.5).

front: Stub generator: lecture calls them generic "RPC package tools"; what does Birrell & Nelson name the tool, and from what input?
back: Lupine, which generated the stubs from Mesa interface modules. (Sec. 1.5)

front: Birrell & Nelson: what happens if user and server are linked directly on one machine, without the stubs?
back: The program would still work.

front: Steps in RPC: name the first step (binding) and what it does.
back: Binding: the client finds and discovers the server that supports the needed functionality. For connection-based protocols (e.g. TCP/IP), the actual connection is established in this step.

front: Steps in RPC: list the full sequence from the client making the call to the client getting the result.
back:
1. Client makes the RPC call; control passes to the stub, blocking the client.
  2. Client stub creates a buffer and marshals the arguments into it.
  3. RPC runtime sends the message to the server via the protocol agreed at binding (TCP, UDP, or shared memory IPC if client and server are on the same machine).
  4. Server RPC runtime receives it and determines which server stub to deliver it to; access control checks can also happen here.
  5. Server stub unmarshals the data into the proper data structures.
  6. The actual server procedure is called.
  7. The server computes the result, which goes to the server stub and back to the client.

front: Marshaling: define it and say why it is needed.
back: Marshaling is the client stub creating a data buffer and populating it with the passed arguments. It is needed because arguments may sit in noncontiguous memory in the client address space, but the transport level requires a single contiguous buffer for transmission.

front: Unmarshalling (server side): what does the server stub do with the received buffer?
back: It extracts the necessary byte sequences from the buffer and populates the appropriate data structures, allocating and initializing the argument variables, so the actual procedure call can be made.

front: Steps in RPC: what must the server do before any client can bind to it?
back: A registration step: the server lets the world know what procedures it supports, what arguments they require, and at what location it can be contacted.

front: IDL: why can't the client and server just be developed together, and what does an IDL provide?
back: They can be written by different developers in different languages, so there must be an agreement letting the server state what procedures it supports and what arguments it requires, so the client can decide which server to bind with. The interface definition language (IDL) is the protocol for expressing that agreement.

front: IDL: standardizing the interface representation enables what runtime feature?
back: It lets the RPC runtime include tools that automate generating the stub functionality.

front: Specifying an IDL: what is the minimum information an interface definition includes?
back: The name of the procedure, the types of the different arguments, and the result type.

front: IDL version numbers: what two purposes do they serve?
back:
• When multiple servers provide the same procedure, the version helps clients find the most up-to-date one.
  • They let a client identify the server whose version fits the rest of the client program.
This supports incremental upgrades: clients and servers need not all be upgraded at the same time.

front: IDL kinds: contrast language-agnostic and language-specific IDLs with an example of each.
back:
• Language-agnostic: SunRPC uses XDR, separate from any programming language.
  • Language-specific: Java RMI uses Java.
Language-specific is great if you know the language; a language-agnostic IDL is simpler to learn than a whole new language.

text: The IDL is used solely to define the {{c1::interface}}; it helps generate {{c2::stubs}}, marshaling procedures, and service-discovery information, and is not used for the {{c3::implementation}} of the service.

front: XDR acronym: what does XDR stand for and who uses it?
back: eXternal Data Representation; it is the language-agnostic IDL used by SunRPC.

front: Marshaling the add example: what must the contiguous buffer hold, and who generates it?
back: A descriptor for the procedure (add) to call on the server plus the arguments i and j. The buffer is generated by the marshaling code.

front: Marshaling: what does it mean that marshaling "encodes into an agreed upon format"?
back: It encodes the data so the server can correctly interpret it; the encoding specifies the layout of the data when serialized into a byte stream.

front: Marshaling an array (the array_add example): why must the serialization convention be agreed in advance?
back: An array can be serialized in more than one way: write the length first then the elements, or write the elements followed by a terminator (as strings do with the null character). Both endpoints must agree on the convention so the receiver can recover the structure.

front: Unmarshalling: how does the code know which bytes to extract from the buffer?
back: Based on the procedure descriptor and the argument types that procedure requires, it extracts the correct chunks of bytes and uses them to initialize data structures matching the argument types. The result: i and j allocated in the server address space, initialized to the values the client placed in the buffer.

front: Marshaling/unmarshalling routines: who writes them and how are they produced?
back: Not the programmer; RPC systems include a special compiler that takes the IDL specification and generates the marshaling/unmarshalling routines. These also perform the encoding-related actions, such as how an array is laid out in the byte stream or converting integers between endiannesses. The programmer just links these autogenerated files with their program.

front: Binding: what two things does it determine for the client?
back:
• Which server to connect to, based on service name and version number.
  • How to connect: the IP address and/or network protocol needed to establish the client/server connection.

front: Registry: what is it and what does it return (the "yellow pages" analogy)?
back: A registry is systems software maintaining a database of all available services. You pass it a service name and version and get back the contact information of the best matching server (matched on protocol, version number, proximity, and so on): IP address, port, and transport protocol.

front: Registry design spectrum: contrast the two extremes.
back:
• Distributed online platform where any RPC service can register.
  • A dedicated process on every server machine that knows only that machine's processes; then clients must already know the host's machine address, and the registry need only provide the service's port number.

front: Registry naming protocol: contrast the simplest scheme with a more sophisticated one.
back: Simplest: the client must specify the exact service name and version number. More sophisticated: the scheme can consider synonyms, so requesting sum might still return the add service.

front: Grapevine: lecture presents the registry abstractly; where does Birrell & Nelson actually do binding, and how is it structured?
back: Through the Grapevine distributed database, replicated across several servers rather than running per-machine (Sec. 2.1, 2.2).

front: Birrell & Nelson binding: how does a client name the interface it imports, by type vs instance?
back: A client binds an importer to an exporter, naming the interface by type (which abstract interface) and instance (which particular implementor). An importer that gives only the type is bound to the closest running instance (Sec. 2.2).

front: Birrell & Nelson: what effect does importing have on the exporter, and when is a binding implicitly broken?
back: Importing has no effect on the exporter's data structures (matters for servers with hundreds of users). A binding is implicitly broken when the exporter crashes and restarts, because a per-export unique identifier is re-checked on every call (Sec. 2.3).

front: Visual metaphor (toy shop outsourcing directory): what three questions does the manager ask, and what does each map to in RPC binding?
back:
• Who provides the service: look up the registry by service name (e.g. an image processing service) to find the servers.
  • Service details: the registry describes each server's services and version numbers, expressed in an IDL.
  • Shipping options (e.g. UPS): the protocols a server supports, such as TCP or UDP.
The application uses all of this to decide which server to bind with.

front: Pointers in a local procedure: why are pointer arguments fine there but nonsensical in RPC?
back: Locally the pointer references an address in the shared address space of caller and callee, so it dereferences fine. In RPC the pointer points to data in the caller's address space but to arbitrary data in the remote address space.

front: Pointers in RPC: what are the two solutions, and how does the pointer-allowing one work?
back:
• Disallow pointers as arguments to any RPC procedure.
  • Allow pointers but marshal the referenced data (not the pointer) into the buffer; on the server, after unpacking, the unmarshalling code passes the address of that data to the local procedure. This "passes" a pointer between client and server.

front: Pointers: lecture solves pointer passing in the runtime; how does Birrell & Nelson handle it instead?
back: It rules it out at stub-generation time: the programmer must avoid arguments or results incompatible with the lack of a shared address space, and Lupine checks this avoidance. The paper discards emulating a shared address space as too expensive for its hardware (Sec. 1.4, 1.5).

front: Partial failures: if the RPC runtime adds timeout/retry mechanisms, is a hung call guaranteed to be resolved or diagnosed?
back: No. Even with timeout/retry there is no guarantee that the problem will be resolved, or that the runtime will gain better insight into what went wrong. Pinpointing the exact cause is in principle too complex, adds a lot of overhead, and is still unlikely to give a definitive answer.

front: Partial failures: what does the RPC system's special error notification actually tell you?
back: It is a catch-all capturing that something went wrong without the exact detail, covering all types of (partial) failures. It can also signal a genuinely partial failure, where the call did not cleanly fail and the client cannot tell what succeeded and what did not.

front: Partial failures: given only a timeout, what can the runtime conclude went wrong?
back: Only that the failure was any of the listed causes (lost client packet, lost server packet, downed network link, downed server machine, failed server process, overloaded server process), possibly several at once. It cannot single out a cause.

front: Call semantics guarantee: lecture gives a vague catch-all error; what exact guarantee does Birrell & Nelson's packet-level protocol define?
back: If the call returns to the user, the server procedure was invoked exactly once; otherwise an exception is reported and the procedure was invoked either once or not at all. The user is not told which, nor whether the fault was a server crash or a communication failure (Sec. 3.1).

front: Birrell & Nelson: what is the primary way clients tell a remote call apart from a local one?
back: The "call failed" exception (Sec. 3.4).

front: RPC design space: what four design choices does the lecture summarize, and what are the options for each?
back:
• Binding: distributed registry or per-machine registry.
  • IDL: language-agnostic or language-specific.
  • Pointers: disallowed, or allowed with the pointed-to data serialized.
  • Partial failures: a special error that tries to capture what went wrong, without guaranteeing a precise answer.

front: SunRPC: who built it, for what, and when?
back: Sun, in the 1980s, originally for its Network File System (NFS) on UNIX; now widely available on other platforms.

front: SunRPC design choices: registry assumption, language assumption, and pointer handling.
back:
• Assumes the server machine is known up front, so there is a registry per machine; the client first talks to that machine's registry.
  • No assumption about client/server programming language; uses the language-agnostic IDL XDR for both interface and data encoding.
  • Allows pointers and serializes the pointed-to data.

front: SunRPC error handling: what retry behavior does it provide?
back: A retry mechanism to re-contact a server when a request times out, with a specifiable number of retries; the runtime tries to return meaningful errors as often as possible.

front: SunRPC errors: what cases do its meaningful errors let a caller distinguish?
back:
• Server unavailable.
  • Mismatch or unsupported protocol or version.
  • A timeout-related failure that covers all other types of failures.

front: Call semantics: SunRPC retries a timed-out call a bounded number of times. What semantics does blind retransmission give, and what does Birrell & Nelson's protocol do differently?
back: Blind retransmission of the whole call gives only at-least-once semantics, unsafe for non-idempotent procedures. The paper's protocol pairs retransmission with call identifiers and a per-activity sequence number so the callee discards duplicates, preserving the exactly-once-on-return guarantee (Sec. 3.1, 3.2).

front: ONC RPC (RFC 1831 Sec. 4): how do transport choices map to call semantics?
back:
• Unreliable transport: a reply implies the procedure ran at least once.
  • A remembered transaction ID can give some degree of at-most-once.
  • Only a reliable transport yields exactly once.

front: SunRPC overview: in what file and language does the server specify its interface, and what compiler processes it?
back: A .x file written in XDR; SunRPC's compiler rpcgen compiles the interface into language-specific stubs for client and server.

front: SunRPC overview: what does the per-machine registry track, and how does a client get a service's contact info?
back: On start the server registers with the local registry daemon, which keeps the service name, version, protocol, and port number. A client must explicitly contact the registry on the target machine to obtain the full contact information.

front: SunRPC: what is the RPC handle and when is it created?
back: When binding happens, the client creates an RPC handle used for every subsequent RPC call, letting the RPC runtime track all RPC-related state on a per-client basis.

front: SunRPC: what is RPC when client and server run on the same machine?
back: It works like other forms of IPC, but with higher-level semantics: procedure call semantics.

front: TI-RPC: what is it, and how does it differ from the original SunRPC?
back: Transport-independent RPC, the name used in Oracle's SunRPC documentation (Oracle bought Sun in 2010). The client/server protocol need not be specified at compile time and can be chosen dynamically at run time; otherwise it closely follows the original SunRPC specification and the XDR IDL.

front: SunRPC XDR example: what procedure does the sample .x file define, with what argument and result types?
back: SQUARE_PROC, taking one argument of type square_in and returning square_out. Both are structs defined in the .x file, each with one int member (a 32-bit integer, as in C). The service squares an integer the client sends.

front: SunRPC XDR: what identifiers does the .x file specify for the service and procedures?
back:
• Service name (SQUARE_PROG) used by clients to find a service.
  • Per-procedure ID number used internally by the runtime.
  • A version applying to the whole collection of procedures.
  • A service id number used by the runtime to differentiate services.

front: SunRPC XDR example: which identifiers does the client use for a service, and which does the RPC runtime use?
back:
• Client: service name, procedure name, and version number.
  • RPC runtime: service id, procedure id, and version id.

front: SunRPC XDR example: what are the procedure ID, the version, and the service id of SQUARE_PROC/SQUARE_PROG?
back: Procedure ID 1, version 1, service id 0x31230000.

front: SunRPC service id: what range must a user-defined service id fall in, and what are the other values for?
back: 0x20000000 to 0x3fffffff (ONC RPC standard). The remaining values are predefined for specific services, such as the network file system, or reserved for future use.

front: SunRPC XDR example: is the procedure name sent between client and server?
back: No. The packets carry the procedure ID, which the runtime uses to identify the procedure being called; the programmer does not use the ID.

front: SunRPC versions: what happens if a client requests a version the server does not support, and why may a server support several versions?
back: The server can reject the communication. A server can support multiple versions of the same procedure, so a procedure can be refined, or new procedures added, without upgrading all clients and servers at the same time.

front: Compiling XDR: what command generates the C client/server stubs from <interface>.x?
back: rpcgen -C <interface>.x

front: Compiling XDR: what does each generated file contain? (.h, _svc.c, _clnt.c, _xdr.c)
back:
• <interface>.h: language-specific datatype definitions and function prototypes.
  • <interface>_svc.c: server-side stub.
  • <interface>_clnt.c: client-side stub.
  • <interface>_xdr.c: marshaling/unmarshalling routines used by both client and server.

front: Compiling XDR: what two parts make up <interface>_svc.c?
back:
• The server main, including the registration step and housekeeping.
  • The RPC-service code that handles request parsing and argument marshaling.
It also includes the prototype for the actual server procedure, which the developer must implement.

front: Compiling XDR: what does the client stub provide, and what is left to the developer?
back: The client stub includes an autogenerated procedure that wraps the actual RPC call the client makes; the developer then just calls that function. On the server, the developer must implement the actual procedure.

front: Compiling XDR: for SQUARE_PROC version 1, what are the generated client wrapper and the server procedure the developer implements, and what does _1 mean?
back:
• Server procedure (developer implements): square_proc_1_svc.
  • Client wrapper (autogenerated): square_proc_1, which makes the RPC that ends in square_proc_1_svc being called.
_1 is the version number. The client just calls y = square_proc_1(x, ...), like a regular procedure call: no sockets, no buffers, no copying. (The lecture writes squareproc_1/squareproc_1_svc; rpcgen uses the lowercased procedure name plus the version.)

front: XDR compilation summary: what does the generated code let the client and server developers do? (diagram)
back: The autogenerated stubs and XDR routines handle marshaling, request parsing, and registration, so developers link them and implement only the client call site and the server procedure. Both sides include the generated .h and link the stub objects; the RPC runtime, called from the stubs, handles OS interaction, sockets, and connections.

front: rpcgen thread safety: is the default code thread safe, and what flag changes that?
back:
By default rpcgen generates non-thread-safe code. Use 
rpcgen -C -M <interface>.x
The -M flag ensures the produced code is thread safe; it does not by itself give a multithreaded server.

front: rpcgen thread safety: why is the default generated code not thread safe, and how does the -M wrapper differ?
back: By default the generated function and the runtime use statically allocated data structures for the result, so concurrent RPC calls from multiple threads race. With -M, square_proc_1 still exists but has a different signature and implementation, e.g. it dynamically allocates memory for the results.

front: rpcgen: how do you actually get a multithreaded server?
back: On Solaris, pass the -A flag. On Linux, a multithreaded server must be implemented manually.

front: rpcgen quiz: what is the return type of square_proc_1 when square.x is compiled with rpcgen -C, and with rpcgen -C -M?
back:
• -C: square_out *, as in square_out *square_proc_1(square_in *, CLIENT *); the result lives in statically allocated storage.
  • -C -M: enum clnt_stat, as in enum clnt_stat square_proc_1(square_in *, square_out *, CLIENT *); the caller supplies a pointer to where the result is written, and the return value is the RPC call status.

front: SunRPC registry: who writes the code the server needs to register with the registry?
back: Nobody by hand: it is autogenerated as part of the rpcgen compilation step.

front: SunRPC registry: what is the per-machine registry process called, and how do you start it on Linux?
back:
portmapper. Start it with 
sudo /sbin/portmap
Both the server (to register) and the client (to find contact info) must contact it.

front: SunRPC portmapper: what does a client already know when it contacts portmapper, and what does it learn from it?
back: It already knows the server machine's IP address (it contacted that machine's RPC daemon). From portmapper it learns the port number to talk to the server and whether the required version and protocol are supported.

front: SunRPC registry: what command lists running services, and what does it return?
back:
/usr/sbin/rpcinfo -p
It returns the program id, version, protocol, socket port number, and service name for every service on that machine.

front: SunRPC registry: on what port and protocols is portmapper itself registered?
back: Socket port 111, registered with both TCP and UDP.

front: SunRPC binding: what is the signature of the client binding call, and what does it return?
back:
CLIENT* clnt_create(char* host, unsigned long prog, unsigned long vers, char* proto);
It returns the client handle used in every subsequent RPC call; the handle also tracks request status and handles error or authentication information.

front: SunRPC binding: in the SQUARE example, where do SQUARE_PROG and SQUARE_VERS come from?
back:
They are autogenerated from compiling the XDR file and included in the header as #define'd values. Example call: 
clnt_handle = clnt_create(rpc_host_name, SQUARE_PROG, SQUARE_VERS, "tcp");

front: SunRPC binding: what must a client do to use a different version of a service?
back: Be recompiled: the version (SQUARE_VERS) is a static #define from the generated header. None of the other client code has to change.

front: XDR data types: name the default scalar types and the two special integer/float widths.
back: Defaults include char, byte, int, float. hyper is a 64-bit integer; quadruple is a 128-bit float. XDR also supports const, compiled into a C #define.

front: XDR quadruple: the lecture calls it a 120-bit float; what is it really?
back: 128 bits (16 bytes). XDR (RFC 4506 Sec. 4.8) and the Sun/Oracle XDR docs both define quadruple-precision floating point as 128 bits using the IEEE format.

front: XDR opaque type: what is it for?
back: Uninterpreted binary data, similar to the C byte type; e.g. an image can be represented as an array of opaque elements.

front: XDR arrays: how are fixed-length and variable-length arrays written, and what struct does a variable-length array compile to?
back: Fixed: int data[80]. Variable: int data<80>, where 80 is the maximum expected length, not the actual one. A variable-length array compiles to a struct with two fields: an integer len (actual size) and a pointer val (address of the data).

front: XDR fixed-length array (int data[80]): what does the fixed size let the runtime do?
back: Know how much memory to allocate whenever arguments of this type are sent or received, and exactly how many bytes to read from the incoming packet stream.

front: XDR variable-length array: how does the receiver recover the data?
back: The sender sets len and points val at the data. The receiver, expecting a variable-length structure, reads the first four bytes for the length, allocates that much memory, and copies the remaining incoming bytes into the buffer.

front: XDR strings: how are they stored in memory vs on the wire?
back: A variable-length string compiles to a C char *. In memory it is stored as a normal null-terminated string, because operations like strcpy and strlen need that representation. Encoded for transmission, it is a pair of len and data, like other variable-length types. Strings are the exception to the usual variable-length-array handling.

front: XDR variable-length array sizing: in-memory size of a full int array of max size 5 on a 32-bit machine?
back: 28 bytes: len (4) + val pointer (4) + five 4-byte ints (20).

front: XDR routines: where are marshaling/unmarshalling routines found, and what cleanup does the compiler generate?
back: In <interface>_xdr.c. The compiler also generates cleanup like xdr_free to free memory allocated by RPC operations.

front: XDR *_freeresult: what is it and who calls it?
back: A user-defined procedure where the user specifies which pieces of state to deallocate after an RPC request is serviced (it uses routines like xdr_free). The RPC runtime automatically calls it after computing the results.

front: Encoding: why is passing the procedure arguments alone not enough?
back: The server can support multiple programs, versions, and procedures, so the request must also identify, in a header, which procedure and version is meant.

front: Encoding: besides the arguments/results, what metadata must an RPC request header carry?
back: The service procedure id, version number, and request id (so repeated requests on retries can be detected); the same header is included in the server's response.

front: Encoding: is there always a 1-1 mapping between in-memory and on-wire representation?
back: Not necessarily; there may be, but what matters is that the data is encoded in a standard format both client and server can deserialize.

front: Encoding: what must precede the RPC packet before it can be sent along the wire?
back: The transport header (TCP/UDP), so the packet is sent in accordance with those transmission protocols.

front: XDR encoding: what alignment, byte order, and number formats does it mandate?
back:
• All data types encoded in multiples of four bytes (a single byte takes the byte plus 3 bytes padding).
  • Big endian is the transmission standard; data is converted to big endian before transmission regardless of host endianness.
  • Two's complement integers; IEEE format for floating point.

front: XDR encoding: why pad to 4-byte multiples, and what is the cost and the benefit of always using big endian on the wire?
back:
• Padding helps alignment when moving data between memory, network packets, and the network card.
  • Big endian: when both machines are little endian the conversion is pure overhead, but the standard means there is never any ambiguity about the wire encoding.

front: XDR encoding example: a variable-length string (max 10) holds "hello". How many bytes in a C process's memory, and how many on the wire?
back:
• Memory: 6 bytes (5 characters + null terminator).
  • Wire: 12 bytes: 4 for the length (5), 5 for h-e-l-l-o (the null terminator is not transmitted), and 3 bytes of padding to the 4-byte boundary.

front: XDR encoding: on-the-wire size of a full variable-length int array of five elements, and why it differs from in-memory?
back: 24 bytes: 4 for the length plus five 4-byte ints (20); no padding since all fields are already multiples of four, and this excludes any RPC/protocol header. In memory it is 28 bytes because the wire form carries the length and data but not the pointer.

front: Java RMI: what is it, who built it, and why "method invocation" instead of "procedure call"?
back: Java Remote Method Invocations, pioneered by Sun for client/server communication among address spaces in the JVM. Java is object-oriented and entities interact via method invocations, not procedure calls, so it is RMI rather than RPC.

front: Java RMI: what is its IDL, and what is the server-side stub called?
back: The IDL is language-specific to Java (all clients and servers are written in Java, and RMI targets JVM address spaces). The server-side stub is called a skeleton.

front: Java RMI runtime: what are its two components and what does each do?
back:
• Remote Reference Layer: common code for reference semantics, e.g. unicast vs broadcast, and return semantics like return-first-response and return-if-all-match.
  • Transport Layer: transport protocol functionality (TCP, UDP, shared memory, etc.).

front: Java RMI: why is the Remote Reference Layer separate from the Transport Layer?
back: Reference semantics are implemented the same way regardless of the transport protocol. A developer can just specify the desired reference semantics, or, for something exotic, implement only this layer while the rest of the system stays the same.
